title: Friends Abroad, a Trap at Home
sum: Jonathan, now high priest and master of Judea, sends envoys to renew the treaty with Rome and writes to Sparta, claiming that Spartans and Jews are brothers, both of Abraham's family. He copies an old letter from the Spartan king Areus to the high priest Onias. In the same letter he says that the Jews need no allies, "since the holy books in our hands give us encouragement", and that their help comes from Heaven.

At home Jonathan drives off Demetrius's army in the far north, raids the Zabadeans and marches through Damascus, while Simon seizes Joppa. They wall off the Seleucid Citadel in Jerusalem to starve it. Then Tryphon, who means to seize the throne from the boy king Antiochus VI, lures Jonathan into Ptolemais with flattery and a promise of the city, kills his men and takes him prisoner. Israel mourns, and the nations around close in.
readings: Read as diplomacy

The chapter shows how a small nation survived between empires: treaties with distant powers (Rome, Sparta) and shrewd use of the Seleucid civil war. Its documents are presented as copied from archives, and much of the chapter's value for historians lies in them.
Read as a warning

Placed side by side, Jonathan's confident letter ("we need none of this", 12:9) and his fatal trust in Tryphon (12:46) make a lesson the book's readers knew from the Psalms: do not rely on nobles (Psalm 146:3).

views.C: The Latin of the Vulgate, which Catholics used for centuries, is the Old Latin, not Jerome's revision; it reads "Arius" for Areus and "Caphetetha" for Chaphenatha.
views.P: Protestant historians prized chapters like this one as the best account of the years between the Testaments; Humphrey Prideaux's The Old and New Testament Connected (1716–1718) built its history of the Maccabees on them.
views.H: Historians debate the letters. Many accept the embassy to Rome as real, since it fits Roman practice and Josephus also records it. The Spartan letters are more doubted, especially Areus's (12:20–23); Erich Gruen argued that the kinship claim was a Jewish construction to win standing in the Greek world. The capture of Jonathan is told plainly and is generally accepted.
views.J: Josephus retells the chapter closely and adds a fuller version of Areus's letter (Antiquities 12.225–227; 13.163–212). The idea that Spartans and Jews were kin through Abraham shows how Jews of the time placed themselves among the peoples of the Greek world.

deep.b:
Three pieces of evidence must be weighed. Areus's letter (12:20–23) would date from about 300 BC, when Areus I ruled Sparta and Onias I was high priest. Its Greek in 1 Maccabees has passed into Hebrew and back again, so its wording tells little. Its claim that Spartans and Jews are both "of Abraham's family" fits a Greek custom of finding kinship between peoples, and Jewish writers of the time linked Abraham's descendants with far-off nations (Josephus, Antiquities 1.239–241).

Jonathan's letter (12:6–18) is built like a Greek diplomatic letter, with a greeting, a reminder of the old friendship, and the envoys' names. The Spartan reply to Simon (14:20–23) has the form of a Spartan public decree. Many historians therefore accept a real exchange in the 140s BC, while doubting Areus's letter; others, such as Goldstein and Katzoff, defend them; still others think the whole dossier was composed in Judea. The Sparta link also appears independently in 2 Maccabees 5:9, where Jason flees there "because of their kinship", so the idea was older than 1 Maccabees.

deep.title: Claude's reading: two kinds of help
deep.b: The chapter sets two scenes side by side. In his letter Jonathan says that the Jews "need none of this" because they have the holy books and "the help from Heaven" (12:9, 15). Thirty verses later he "trusted" Tryphon (12:46) and walks into the trap. The narrator makes no comment, but the order of the scenes may be a quiet judgment: help from Heaven was enough; trust in a Greek general was not. This is Claude's own reading. It overlaps with scholars who find the book ambivalent about foreign alliances, but none that I can cite makes this exact link.

echoes: Genesis 25:1–4; Genesis 17:4–5; 2 Maccabees 5:9; 1 Kings 22:4; Ezra 6:10; Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 9:2; Psalm 83:4; Psalm 146:3; 1 Kings 19:10

settings.what: The envoys' speech to the Roman Senate
settings.to: the Roman Senate in its council chamber
settings.when: about 144 BC, soon after Jonathan had backed Antiochus VI
settings.why: To renew the treaty Judas had made in 161 BC (8:17–32), so that Rome would count Jonathan's Judea among its friends.
settings.readers: 1 Maccabees was most likely written in Hebrew in Judea around 100 BC, late in John Hyrcanus's reign or early in Alexander Jannaeus's (see 16:24), so its first hearers lived under the later Hasmoneans, while Rome was still a friend. No copy has been found at Qumran, and the Hebrew is lost; Origen gives its Semitic title, and Jerome says he found it in Hebrew. The Greek translation, the text translated here, was read by Greek-speaking Jews (Josephus used it in the AD 90s) and then by Christians.
views: Many date the book around 100 BC, late in John Hyrcanus's reign or early in Alexander Jannaeus's, from the reference to John Hyrcanus's annals (16:24).
Some date it within John Hyrcanus's lifetime, perhaps the 120s BC, reading 16:23–24 as a reference to annals still being kept.

settings.by: Jonathan the high priest, with the council of elders, the priests and the people
settings.to: the rulers and people of Sparta
settings.when: about 144 BC, with the embassy to Rome
settings.why: To renew an old friendship and claim kinship with the most famous city of Greece, while telling the Spartans that the Jews need no military help.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers the letter showed their ruling family speaking as equals with the old Greek world, and saying in the same breath that their trust was in the holy books and in Heaven (12:9, 15).

settings.by: Areus, king of Sparta, as the text presents it
settings.when: about 300 BC, if it is genuine
settings.why: To declare that Spartans and Jews are brothers of Abraham's family and to offer friendship.
settings.readers: Readers in Hasmonean Judea heard an old proof that the Jews had been honored by Greeks long before the troubles of their own day. Whether the letter is authentic is debated (see the deep section).
views: A real letter of about 300 BC, preserved in Jerusalem's archives (Goldstein).
A Jewish composition, written to give the friendship with Sparta a past (Gruen and others).

settings.when: about 143 BC, when Tryphon was planning to seize the throne
settings.why: To persuade Jonathan to send away his army and come to Ptolemais with only a few men.
settings.readers: The book's readers knew the end of the story. The speech teaches them how Seleucid courtesy could hide a trap, a lesson repeated when Antiochus VII breaks his word (15:27).

settings.when: after Jonathan's capture
settings.why: To call for a war of extermination while the Jews have no leader.
settings.readers: For Jews in Judea about 100 BC, surrounded by Greek cities that had long been hostile (5:1–2), the boast named a real fear, which Simon's rise in the next chapter answers.

title: The Last Brother
sum: With Jonathan a prisoner, the people panic. Simon, the last of Mattathias's sons, calls them to Jerusalem: his brothers have all died for Israel, and he will not spare himself. The people make him their leader. Tryphon demands a ransom and two of Jonathan's sons as hostages; Simon pays, knowing it is a trick, so that no one can blame him. Tryphon keeps the money, is stopped by snow, and kills Jonathan in Gilead. Simon brings his brother's bones home and builds the family a monument of seven pyramids at Modein.

Tryphon murders the boy king and takes the crown. Simon turns to Demetrius II, who cancels Judea's taxes, and the book declares: "In the year 170 the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from Israel" (142 BC). Contracts are now dated by Simon's years. He takes a fortified city by siege, cleanses it and settles it with Jews, and in 141 BC the starving Seleucid garrison in Jerusalem's Citadel surrenders. Simon enters it with palm branches and music and makes the day a yearly feast.
readings: Read as a founding story

The chapter tells how an independent Jewish state began: a leader chosen by acclamation, the end of tribute, a new system of dating, and the fall of the last foreign fortress in Jerusalem. Each step is the kind of event a dynasty remembers.
Read as Scripture's pattern

The book tells it in the language of Israel's earlier histories: "I alone am left" (Elijah), bones brought home (Joseph, Saul and Jonathan), a yoke broken (Leviticus 26:13; Isaiah 10:27), idols removed and a city cleansed (Josiah). The writer wants readers to hear God's old promises in a political event, though he does not say so.

views.P: Luther, in his preface to the book, praised 1 Maccabees as close in its words and speeches to the books of Scripture and useful for understanding Daniel, while not counting it among them. Many Protestant readers have valued chapters like this one as a model of courage and leadership.
views.H: Historians accept the main events: Jonathan's death about 143 BC, Simon's turn to Demetrius II, the remission of tribute in 142 BC and the fall of the Citadel in 141 BC. Josephus and the rabbinic Scroll of Fasts confirm the date of the Citadel's fall. Most scholars correct "Gaza" in 13:43 to Gazara (see the variant). Many note the book's care to defend Simon's payment of the ransom (13:17–18) and his building of a Greek-style tomb.
views.J: The Scroll of Fasts (Megillat Ta'anit) keeps 23 Iyyar as a day of joy, when "the men of the Citadel went out of Jerusalem". The rabbis also remembered the Hasmonean custom of dating documents by the high priest's years and said the sages abolished it (Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 18b).

deep.b:
What did "the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted" (13:41) mean in practice? Demetrius II, in his letter, confirmed the earlier grants, cancelled the crown tax and every other toll, pardoned the Jews' support for Tryphon, and let them keep their fortresses (13:36–40). Judea paid no tribute and had no royal garrison except in the Citadel, which fell the next year. The people began to date contracts "in the first year of Simon" (13:42), as one would date by a king's reign.

But Judea was not yet free of the Seleucids. Antiochus VII soon claimed Joppa, Gazara and the Citadel back (15:28–31), and after Simon's death he besieged Jerusalem and forced John Hyrcanus to pay tribute again (Josephus, Antiquities 13.236–248). Full independence came only after Antiochus VII died in 129 BC. The book chooses 142 BC as the turning point because it was the year of Simon.

deep.h: A Greek tomb for the Maccabees
deep.b: Simon's monument at Modein (13:27–30) had seven pyramids, tall columns, carved suits of armor and ships, polished stone, and was meant to be seen from afar. This was the style of the great tombs of the Hellenistic world, like the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus. Josephus saw it in his day (Antiquities 13.211–212). Historians often point out the irony: the family that had fought Greek ways honored its dead in a Greek way. The book sees no problem. The carved ships celebrate the new port at Joppa (14:5), and the monument stands "to this day" (13:30), a claim of permanence for the family's rule.

echoes: 1 Kings 19:4; 1 Kings 19:10; 2 Samuel 21:12–14; Genesis 50:25; Leviticus 26:13; Isaiah 10:27; Genesis 27:40; Deuteronomy 7:5; 2 Kings 23:4–14; 1 Chronicles 15:16; John 12:13

settings.to: the frightened people gathered in Jerusalem
settings.when: about 143 BC, after Jonathan's capture, as Tryphon's army approaches
settings.why: To rally the people by recalling his family's sacrifices and pledging his own life, and so to take the leadership in a crisis.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, under the later Hasmoneans, the speech is the founding pledge of the ruling house: the family that gave its sons for the law and the sanctuary (13:3–4) earned its rule.

settings.when: in answer to his speech
settings.why: To make Simon their leader in place of Judas and Jonathan and promise obedience.
settings.readers: The acclamation answered anyone who asked by what right a priestly family outside the line of Zadok ruled: the people themselves chose it, as they would again in 140 BC (14:35, 41).

settings.when: as Tryphon advances with Jonathan as prisoner
settings.why: To get money and hostages while keeping Jonathan, and to put Simon in an impossible position.
settings.readers: The book's readers saw why Simon paid: the narrator explains that refusal would have brought blame for Jonathan's death (13:17–18). Some scholars think the explanation answers critics of Simon in the author's own day.

settings.to: Simon the high priest, the elders and the Jewish nation
settings.when: 142 BC, while Demetrius was at war with Tryphon
settings.why: To win Simon's support by confirming his fortresses, cancelling the crown tax and other tolls, and pardoning past offenses.
settings.readers: For readers about 100 BC this document was the legal basis of their freedom from tribute, and the book places it just before the cry "the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted" (13:41).

settings.by: the people of Israel, in their contracts
settings.when: from 142 BC
settings.why: To date legal documents by Simon's years, a sign of self-rule.
settings.readers: Readers would have known contracts dated this way; the rabbis later remembered and abolished a similar Hasmonean formula (Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 18b).

settings.by: the people of the city Simon besieged
settings.when: as the siege tower breaks into the city
settings.why: To ask for mercy rather than punishment.
settings.readers: The plea is in biblical language ("not as our evil deeds deserve", compare Psalm 103:10), and readers would note that Simon spares their lives but not their city.

title: A Song for Simon, a Decree in Bronze
sum: Demetrius II marches east and is captured by the Parthian king. In Judea the land is at rest, and a poem praises Simon in the words of Judges, Leviticus, Micah and Zechariah: peace in the land, crops and fruit, old men in the squares, "each one under his vine and his fig tree", the law searched out and the sanctuary made glorious. Rome and Sparta hear of Jonathan's death and renew their treaties with Simon; Simon sends a great gold shield to Rome.

Then the people, grateful, issue a public decree on bronze tablets set up on Mount Zion (September 140 BC). It reviews what Simon and his brothers did and declares that the Jews and the priests are pleased to have Simon as "leader and high priest forever, until a faithful prophet arises", general, and ruler of the sanctuary, with the sole right to purple and gold. Simon accepts. The chapter is the book's center of gravity: here the Hasmonean house receives its charter.
readings: Read as a political charter

The decree is written like a Greek honorary decree, listing a benefactor's deeds and the honors voted him. It gives the Hasmonean family a legal title to the high priesthood and the rule, grounded in the people's will, the deeds of the brothers and the kings' recognition.
Read as the prophets' hope

The poem borrows the promises of the prophets, so that Simon's peace sounds like the age of blessing. Yet the decree's own words, "until a faithful prophet arises", admit that God has not spoken. The chapter holds praise and caution together.

views.C: Augustine described the age of the rebuilt Temple as a time without prophets, in which the Jews were ruled by priest-princes until Herod, the first king of foreign race, under whom Christ was born, as Genesis 49:10 had foretold (City of God 18.45). He does not discuss 14:41, but his account is the frame in which Catholic readers have long placed the Hasmonean priest-rulers.
views.P: William Whitaker, arguing against the Catholic canon, held that books written after prophecy had ceased could not belong to the Old Testament (Disputation on Holy Scripture, 1588). 14:41 is the kind of evidence such arguments use: the decree itself admits that no prophet was speaking.
views.H: Most historians accept the decree as an authentic document, perhaps shortened, because of its formal style and its date. They read the poem (14:4–15) as court praise in biblical style. Jonathan Goldstein argued that the author meant to present the Hasmoneans as the fulfillment of prophecy; others, such as Joseph Sievers, stress that the decree's clause about the prophet reflects real opposition to the new priestly house.
views.J: Later Jewish tradition was divided about the Hasmoneans. The Talmud tells of a sage who told a Hasmonean king, "Let the crown of kingship be enough for you; leave the crown of priesthood to the seed of Aaron" (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 66a), and Josephus tells the same story of John Hyrcanus and the Pharisees (Antiquities 13.288–292). The Psalms of Solomon accuse the Hasmonean kings of taking David's throne.

deep.b:
The poem of 14:4–15 has no line that quotes a prophet word for word, but almost every line echoes one. "The land was quiet" is the refrain of Judges. "The land gave its crops, and the trees of the plains their fruit" is the blessing of Leviticus 26:4, and "no one was there to frighten them" its sequel (Leviticus 26:6). The old men in the squares come from Zechariah 8:4. "Each one sat under his vine and his fig tree" is Micah 4:4 (and Zechariah 3:10), and also the description of Solomon's golden age (1 Kings 4:25).

Does the book mean that the prophecies were fulfilled? Yes, in part: Goldstein argued that the author, writing for the Hasmonean court, wanted readers to see the age of promise in Simon's reign and to set aside the more radical hopes of books like Daniel. No: others note that the book never uses the language of fulfillment, never calls Simon an anointed one or a son of David (David's throne is mentioned only in Mattathias's speech, 2:57), and that the decree's own words leave room for a prophet still to come (14:41). Christian readers have read Micah 4 and Zechariah 8 of the kingdom Christ brings; Simon's peace was a short one, ended by his murder (16:16) and, within a century, by Rome (63 BC). When and how the promised reign of peace comes is carded at Psalm 72.

The decree (14:27–45) has three parts: the date and assembly (14:27–28); the reasons, a history of the family's deeds (14:29–40); and the resolution, Simon's offices and rights with a penalty clause (14:41–45). Then the people agree and Simon accepts (14:46–47), and the tablets are set up (14:48–49).

Two features stand out. First, the offices are granted "forever" (14:41): the decree founds a dynasty. Second, it joins the high priesthood, the army and the government in one man, "leader and high priest", "general", "ethnarch" (14:41–47). In Israel's history the offices had usually been held by different men (Numbers 27:21; Zechariah 4:14), though Zechariah 6:11–13 and the figure of Melchizedek point the other way, and Israel's historians remembered King Uzziah struck with skin disease for taking a priest's task (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The question "What power may rulers have over the church?" is carded at 2 Chronicles 26. Some Jews of the time objected: the Qumran scrolls' "Wicked Priest" is often identified with Jonathan or Simon (see the hasmoneans topic), and the Pharisees later asked John Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood.

The clause "until a faithful prophet arises" limits the decree. It assumes that no true prophet is speaking (4:46; 9:27) and that one may come. Whether the book's statement that prophets were no longer seen rules it out as Scripture is carded on the book's opening page.

echoes: Judges 3:11; Leviticus 26:4–6; Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10; Zechariah 8:4–5; 1 Kings 4:25; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; Ezra 2:63; Numbers 25:13; Psalm 110:4; Genesis 14:18; 2 Chronicles 26:16–21; John 1:21; Hebrews 7:1–3

settings.what: The poem in praise of Simon
settings.by: the narrator, perhaps quoting a song of the time
settings.when: looking back on Simon's rule, 142–134 BC
settings.why: To describe Simon's reign as a time of peace and blessing in the words of the Law and the Prophets.
settings.readers: Readers under Simon's descendants heard their own state praised in Scripture's language. Readers after 63 BC, when Pompey took Jerusalem, could hear it with sadness; the Psalms of Solomon, written then, blamed the Hasmoneans for the loss.
views: The poem presents Simon's age as the fulfillment of prophecy (Goldstein).
The poem borrows biblical phrases to praise a good ruler, without claiming fulfillment.

settings.by: the rulers and city of Sparta
settings.to: Simon the high priest, the elders, the priests and the Jewish people
settings.when: about 140 BC, after Numenius and Antipater's visit
settings.why: To record the renewal of friendship in Sparta's public archives and send Simon a copy.
settings.readers: For readers in Judea the document proved that the friendship of 12:6–18 had been answered. Many historians think it closer to a real decree than Areus's letter.

settings.when: after the news from Rome and Sparta
settings.why: To ask how to honor Simon and his sons for what they had done.
settings.readers: The question introduces the decree, so that readers see the Hasmonean honors as the people's own gratitude.

settings.by: the great assembly of priests, people, rulers and elders
settings.to: all Judea, on bronze tablets on Mount Zion, with copies in the Temple treasury
settings.when: 18 Elul 172, September 140 BC
settings.why: To confirm Simon as leader, high priest and general forever, until a faithful prophet arises, and to bind every Jew and priest to obey him on pain of punishment.
settings.readers: For readers about 100 BC this was the charter of the ruling house, binding the people and the priests (14:44). It bound every Jew in Judea, and the priests in the Temple, and it answered rival claims to the high priesthood. Its clause about a prophet left room for those who hoped God would decide otherwise.
views: Most historians accept it as an authentic public decree, perhaps abridged.
Some think the author reworked it, especially the clause about the prophet.

title: Promises Made and Broken
sum: Antiochus VII, brother of the captured Demetrius II, writes to Simon from the islands, confirming all the grants of earlier kings, allowing him to mint coins, and declaring Jerusalem and the Temple free. He lands, the army comes over to him, and he besieges Tryphon in Dor. Meanwhile Numenius returns from Rome with a consul's letter to the kings and cities of the east, telling them not to harm the Jews and to hand over fugitives to Simon.

Once Antiochus is strong, he refuses Simon's help, breaks his promises, and demands Joppa, Gazara and the Citadel or a thousand talents. Simon answers that the Jews have taken nothing of anyone else's, only "the inheritance of our ancestors", and offers a hundred talents for two towns. Antiochus is furious. Tryphon escapes by sea, and the king's general Cendebeus fortifies Kedron and begins raiding Judea.
readings: Read as politics
The chapter shows the limits of Judea's new freedom: it depended on Seleucid weakness. Rome's letter gave diplomatic cover but no troops.
Read as a claim to the land
Simon's answer (15:33–35) is the book's clearest statement of why the Hasmoneans took the coastal towns: the land is Israel's inheritance from its fathers, wrongly taken by enemies.

views.H: Historians generally accept Antiochus VII's letter and its later reversal; Josephus tells how the king went on to besiege Jerusalem under John Hyrcanus. Rome's letter (15:16–24) has the form of a real Roman circular, though the consul's identity and its date are debated, and some link it with a similar decree in Josephus (Antiquities 14.145–148). The list of recipients is a valuable map of Jewish communities and Roman friends about 140 BC.
views.J: Josephus retells these events, adding that Antiochus VII later besieged Jerusalem and, during the Feast of Booths, sent sacrifices to the Temple, which won him the name "the Pious" (Antiquities 13.236–248).

deep.b:
Antiochus's envoy says Joppa, Gazara and the Citadel are "towns of my kingdom" (15:28). Simon answers from Scripture: "We hold the inheritance of our ancestors" (15:33). The word klēronomia is the Septuagint's term for the land divided among the tribes (Numbers 26:53–56), and the argument is like Jephthah's answer to the king of Ammon (Judges 11:15–27).

Historically the two claims stand on different ground. Joppa had been a Philistine and Phoenician port and had never been ruled by Israel's kings. Gezer (Gazara) came to Israel only when Pharaoh gave it to Solomon (1 Kings 9:16). But Joshua 13:1–6 counts the whole coast among the land still to be possessed, and Simon reads the promise, not the history, as the title deed. Antiochus reads the treaties. The book leaves no doubt which it accepts, and the next chapter's victory confirms it. How the promise of the land applies today is carded at Numbers 34.

The letter of Lucius (15:16–21) asks the kings and cities of the east to leave the Jews alone and to hand over Jewish fugitives to Simon. It is addressed to Ptolemy VIII of Egypt, and copies go to Demetrius II, Attalus II of Pergamum, Ariarathes V of Cappadocia, the Parthian king, and a long list of cities and islands (15:22–23). Rome made no promise of military help. But in the Greek world a word from Rome mattered, and the letter gave Simon's envoys and the Jews of the diaspora a protector. The places named include several that Acts later mentions as homes of Jewish communities: Cyprus, Cyrene, Pamphylia, Rhodes and Cos (Acts 2:10; Acts 13:4; Acts 21:1).

echoes: Judges 11:15–27; Numbers 26:53–56; Joshua 13:1–6; 1 Kings 9:16; 1 Kings 10:4–5; Acts 2:9–11; Acts 9:1–2; Acts 24:5

settings.by: Antiochus VII, before he had won the throne
settings.to: Simon the high priest and ethnarch, and the Jewish nation
settings.when: 139/138 BC, from the islands, before landing in Syria
settings.why: To win Simon's support against Tryphon by confirming his exemptions, allowing him to mint coins and declaring Jerusalem free.
settings.readers: Readers who knew how soon these promises were broken (15:27) heard the letter as one more example of Seleucid bargaining; the right to mint (15:6) was later used by Simon's successors, whose coins survive (see the note at 15:6).

settings.to: King Ptolemy VIII of Egypt, with copies to other kings and cities
settings.when: about 140–139 BC
settings.why: To declare the Jews Rome's friends and allies, forbid others to make war on them, and order Jewish fugitives handed over to Simon.
settings.readers: For readers before 63 BC, Rome's friendship was a protection, and the list of addressees showed how far that protection seemed to reach. After Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, the letter would likely have read differently.

settings.when: during the siege of Dor, 138 BC
settings.why: To reclaim Joppa, Gazara and the Citadel, or a thousand talents in their place, and so restore Seleucid control.
settings.readers: Readers recognized the claim Seleucid kings would keep pressing; Josephus says Antiochus did later besiege Jerusalem.

settings.when: in Jerusalem, 138 BC
settings.why: To deny that the Jews have taken anyone else's land, to claim the land as their ancestral inheritance, and to offer a token payment for Joppa and Gazara.
settings.readers: For readers in Hasmonean Judea, whose rulers were then conquering Idumea, Samaria and the coast, Simon's words gave a biblical ground for their expansion.

title: Murder at Dok
sum: Old now, Simon hands the war to his sons Judas and John. John leads twenty thousand men against Cendebeus, crosses a stream first when his men hesitate, and routs the enemy as far as Kedron and Azotus. Then Simon's son-in-law Ptolemy son of Abubus, governor of Jericho, plots to seize the country. He invites Simon and two of his sons to a banquet in the little fortress of Dok, and when they are drunk his men kill them. He sends men to kill John too, but a messenger warns John, who seizes and kills the assassins.

The book ends with the formula of the books of Kings: the rest of John's story is written "in the book of the days of his high priesthood." That sentence is the main clue to when 1 Maccabees was written: late in John's high priesthood or soon after his death in 104 BC.
readings: Read as a dynasty's survival
The last of the brothers dies by treachery, as Jonathan did, but the line continues. The book ends with John safe and in command, and the reader knows his long reign followed.
Read as the end of a history
By closing like Kings, the author places his book in the line of Israel's histories, with John Hyrcanus as the next ruler whose deeds are written in official annals.

views.H: Historians read 16:23–24 as the author's own dating clue, placing the book late in John's reign or soon after it (he died in 104 BC). Josephus tells Simon's murder differently: Simon's wife and two sons were taken prisoner, and Ptolemy killed them during John's siege of the fortress (Antiquities 13.228–235). Some scholars think 16:23–24 or even chapters 14–16 were added later, but most take them as original.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition remembered "Yohanan the high priest" for reforms of the tithe laws (Mishnah Ma'aser Sheni 5:15), and also said that he "served as high priest eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee" (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 29a). The Hebrew Sefer Yosippon (southern Italy, 900s AD) retold the Hasmonean story for medieval Jews from Josephus and the Maccabean books.

deep.h: How the book ends, and when it was written
deep.b:
The last two verses copy the closing formula of Kings and Chronicles: "The rest of Solomon's story... is written in the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds, is it not?" (1 Kings 11:41). The Greek idou tauta gegraptai, "look, these are written", is the Septuagint's form of it. The "book of the days" is the Hebrew title of Chronicles, divre hayyamim, "the events of the days", here meaning official annals.

Three clues date the book. (1) It knows the annals of John's high priesthood "from the time he became high priest", which suggests that his rule is over or nearly so (he died in 104 BC). (2) It speaks warmly of Rome, so it was written before Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. (3) Origen gives its Hebrew title (Eusebius, Church History 6.25.2), and Jerome says he found it in Hebrew (Prologus Galeatus), so it was first written in Hebrew. Many therefore place it around 100 BC, late in John Hyrcanus's reign or early in Alexander Jannaeus's; a minority date it earlier. The three Ethiopian books of Meqabyan, despite the name, are different works, not this book.

Judas fell in battle (9:18). Jonathan was taken by deceit and killed (12:48; 13:23). Simon was murdered at a feast by his own son-in-law (16:16). The book uses the word "deceit" (dolos) for both Tryphon's trap and Ptolemy's (13:17, 31; 16:13, 15). The danger to the Hasmonean house now comes from inside the family and from ambition, "his heart grew proud" (16:13), the pride that opened the book in Alexander, whose "heart swelled with pride" (1:3), and in Antiochus IV, who entered the sanctuary "in his arrogance" (1:21). The book does not draw the lesson out, but its readers, living under the later Hasmoneans, whose quarrels finally opened the door to Rome, could.
